summary: This memo proposes a plan for allocating and assigning the network number space, building on RFC 1174. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 2050.

plainLanguage.summary: IP addresses are like phone numbers, and someone must decide who gets which. This paper proposes a plan for handing them out fairly. A later paper replaced it.

questions: guidelines for ip address space management
how are ip addresses allocated geographically
what is a regional internet registry
why are class a addresses scarce
how did ip address management work in the early internet
subtitle: A system for fairly distributing IP addresses across geographic regions.

tldr.problem: Internet growth required a more systematic way to allocate IP network addresses globally rather than having a single central authority.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes creating regional registries in Europe, North America, the Pacific Rim, and Central/South America, each responsible for assigning addresses in their geographic area, while the central Internet Registry retains some reserved blocks.
tldr.outcome: This established the regional registry system that shaped Internet address management for years, though it was later replaced by RFC 2050 as address exhaustion became a more pressing concern.

facts.label: Regional blocks
facts.value: 8 geographic Class C blocks, each 131,072 addresses

facts.label: Proposed regions
facts.value: Europe, North America, Central/South America, Pacific Rim

today: RFC 1466 is Informational and was obsoleted by RFC 2050. It established the geographic regional registry system that managed Internet address allocation for years, but the document itself is no longer the current guidance as address exhaustion and CIDR techniques drove further evolution.

sections.title: The Problem of IP Address Management
sections.content:
As the Internet grew in the early 1990s, demand for network addresses skyrocketed. A single central Internet Registry (IR) could not keep up with requests from all over the world. The RFC notes that the distribution of registration responsibilities is necessary to serve a more diverse, global population better. Rather than waiting for a single registry, local organizations in different geographic areas could issue addresses more efficiently in their own languages and customs, and with knowledge of local network requirements.

The RFC builds on RFC 1174, which first suggested delegating some registration duties to regional bodies. Now it was time to define exactly how that delegation would work, what organizations would qualify, and how the global address space would be divided fairly.
sections.plainLanguage: One person giving out all the phone numbers to the whole world is too slow. It is better to have one person in each country or region do it instead.

sections.title: Qualifications and Responsibilities for Regional Registries
sections.content:
The RFC defines strict criteria for organizations that would become distributed regional registries. They must be recognized and legitimate within their geographic region, well-established with credibility outside the registry role, and willing to commit resources for stable and reliable service. They must also agree to follow allocation guidelines set by the central IANA and Internet Registry, and coordinate with the IR on how to sub-allocate address blocks to smaller organizations.

The text proposes four main geographic regions: Europe, North America, Central/South America, and the Pacific Rim. Each region would get its own registry, with the Internet Registry remaining as a fallback for regions not yet served by a designated authority. This balanced decentralization with coordination, ensuring that local needs were met without allowing chaos.
sections.plainLanguage: A local registry must be trusted, established, and promise to follow the rules set by the main Internet people.

sections.title: How IP Address Classes Are Allocated
sections.content:
IP addresses came in three main classes (A, B, and C), representing increasingly smaller blocks. Class A addresses were rarest and most powerful, Class B were mid-sized, and Class C were plentiful but smaller. The RFC notes that Class A and B networks were running low: only about 126 Class A networks existed, with only 11 unassigned, and fewer than half the Class B space had been allocated.

Because of this scarcity, the RFC proposes that Class A numbers remain entirely under central control, with no delegation to regional registries. Class B numbers would be allocated in small blocks to regional registries under strict conditions. Class C addresses, far more abundant, would be divided into eight geographic blocks, each representing about 6% of the total Class C space, with ranges designated for Europe, North America, Central/South America, the Pacific Rim, and multi-regional or undefined use.
sections.plainLanguage: The three types of addresses are like having different sizes of mailboxes. The smallest and rarest are kept by the main office, the medium ones are given out carefully to regions, and the most common ones are split up geographically.

sections.title: Assignment Rules for Organizations
sections.content:
The RFC sets specific rules for how many Class C addresses an organization would receive based on its projected needs over 24 months. An organization needing fewer than 256 addresses would get one Class C network; one needing 512 to 1,023 would get two contiguous Class C networks; and so on up to 64 contiguous Class C networks for organizations needing 16,384 or more addresses. The intent was to efficiently pack organizations into the address space without wasteful over-allocation.

The registries could deviate from these rules on a case-by-case basis if an organization had special needs, such as multiple geographically separated office LANs. For Class B addresses, organizations had to prove exceptional need: more than 32 subnets and 4,096 hosts, with a detailed engineering plan explaining why Class C networks would not suffice.
sections.plainLanguage: If a company is small, it gets a few address blocks. If it is big, it gets more. Companies must show they really need what they ask for.

sections.title: Legacy and Impact
sections.content:
This RFC established the foundational structure for the regional Internet registry system that served the Internet for over a decade. It introduced the concept of geographic allocation blocks that became the basis for CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) and modern address aggregation. The system successfully distributed the registration burden globally and made address assignment more responsive to local communities.

However, the RFC was replaced by RFC 2050 as concerns about address space exhaustion became more urgent in the mid-1990s. The exhaustion of IPv4 addresses remained a central problem, and later developments like Network Address Translation (NAT) and eventually IPv6 would provide longer-term solutions. RFC 1466 represents an important intermediate step in the evolution of Internet infrastructure management.
sections.plainLanguage: This plan helped organize how addresses were given out, but as the Internet kept growing, an even better system had to be made.

layers.label: Global Authority
layers.detail: IANA and Internet Registry retain oversight and Class A addresses

layers.label: Regional Registries
layers.detail: Four geographic regions handle Class B and Class C allocation

layers.label: Local Organizations
layers.detail: Individual networks receive Class C addresses or larger blocks
